title: Kepler’s laws
target: Use orbital shape, equal areas and period comparisons.
criteria: Place the central body at a focus of an ellipse.
Compare speed near and far from the central body.
Use T²=a³ only with the specified units and central body.

authoring.limitations: Reasoning evidence only. Multiple choice does not certify physical performance. Teacher reviews before assigning and rates mastery separately.

cpa.prompt: Where is the Sun located in the ideal elliptical orbit model?
options: At every point on the orbit.
cpa.guide: Kepler’s first law places the central body at a focus.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: An ellipse has two foci. Must a second star occupy the unused focus of a planetary orbit?
options: No; a focus is a geometric location, not necessarily another object.
Yes; the planet sits permanently at the other focus.
No; elliptical orbits have no foci.
Yes; every ellipse requires two stars.
cpa.guide: Only one focus contains the central body in this ideal model.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

cpa.prompt: Where does an object in an elliptical solar orbit move faster?
options: Its speed is identical everywhere in every ellipse.
cpa.guide: Equal swept areas in equal times require greater speed near perihelion.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

cpa.prompt: Two orbit segments sweep equal areas about the Sun. What does Kepler’s second law say about their elapsed times?
options: The farther segment takes zero time.
The nearer segment always takes twice as long.
cpa.guide: Equal areas correspond to equal times.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: For a Sun-orbit with a in AU and T in years, T² = a³. If a = 9 AU, what is T?
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: Can T² = a³ with AU and years be used unchanged for an orbit around a star with a different mass?
options: Only if distance is written without units.
Yes; changing the name of the star is enough.
No; the central mass changes the proportionality.
cpa.guide: The unit-normalized relation assumes the Sun’s mass; the general law includes central mass.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Select a claim supported by the stated evidence and assumptions.
